title: Cloud, Edge & Platform Engineering
seo_title: Cloud, Edge & Platform Engineering | Dataq Software
meta_description: Cloud, Edge & Platform Engineering services from Dataq Software: scope, delivery pattern, platforms and committed outcomes.

blocks.x: Cloud, Edge & Platform Engineering runs the estate as an economic and reliability system: hybrid placement by policy, golden paths that carry SLOs and budgets by default, edge fleets that survive partitions, and unit costs that fall on a signed trend line — across clouds, without tribal dialects.

The platform domain turns infrastructure into product: golden paths that carry SLOs and budgets by default, runtimes that recover before users notice, and an economics discipline that makes every workload justify its cost. Product teams should ship features, not plumbing.

Seven practices cover modernization, the runtimes themselves, edge where latency lives, reliability engineering, developer experience, FinOps with sustainability, and the mission-critical tier where downtime is measured in regulators' phone calls.

blocks.x: Reliability and unit cost: the numbers the business feels

The platform conversation changed: engineering leaders no longer buy infrastructure, they buy change failure rates and unit costs. The seven practices here are managed on exactly those numbers — SLO adherence, path adoption, placement policy coverage, cost per workload — because those are the numbers the business actually experiences.

The edge adds a discipline the data center never taught: partition-tolerant behavior, store-and-forward resilience, fleet heterogeneity at scale and sites that fail silently. The practices treat edge as a first-class estate with its own gates, not as a cloud region with worse networking.
The domain reference architecture — estate as one system

Placement policy decides where workloads run, golden paths carry how they deploy, SRE discipline decides when they change, and FinOps prices what it all costs — one operating model across clouds, on-prem and the edge, with drift caught by monitors instead of by incidents.
